why: The statement asks whether infinitely many Pell numbers are prime. No event in the record proves or refutes that. The 2001, 2004 and 2009 records are finite prime discoveries or searches, so they are instances. Some of these primes are only probable primes, but that does not change the scope. The three in-window papers are about different questions: the largest prime factor, a primality test on Pell's cubic, and Pell's equation. They are variants. The Dumitru-Prunescu AI disclosure concerns Pell's equation, not this problem, and names no system, so its AI role is none. The Hone-Jeffery-Selcoe conjecture and the knot paper settle nothing about this question, so their scope is none. Broderius-Greene proves finiteness for some Lucas families, and its scope was the close call. The record never shows that (2,-1) lies in either family, and the Pell sequence already has many known primes. So I answered on what the record shows, a theorem about other sequences, and scored it variant. I marked its verification digested on the strength of the journal publication. That choice does not affect the outcome, because a variant is discarded either way.
doubts: The record never read the Broderius-Greene family conditions. If (P,Q)=(2,-1) were inside a finite-primes family, the question would already have a pre-window negative answer. That seems implausible, given that dozens of Pell primes are already known (the record does not give the exact count) and the paper conjectures infinitude for sequences without obvious obstructions, but the record does not confirm it. The frozen list bullet was not read either.
